title: Silane vs Siloxane Sealers: Silane Wins on Dense Concrete
metaDescription: Silane wins on dense concrete driveways because it soaks deeper; siloxane wins on porous brick and block. Most sealers blend both and last 5 to 10 years.
h1: Silane vs Siloxane Sealers: Which One Your Surface Needs
keywords: are siloxane sealers easy to apply
intro:
In the silane vs siloxane matchup, silane wins on dense concrete such as driveways, garage aprons and sidewalks, because its smaller molecule soaks deeper into tight pores. Siloxane wins on porous brick, block and stucco, where its larger molecule bridges big pores and makes rain bead off the wall.

Most sealers on the shelf are a silane-siloxane blend, so the practical question is which one a product leans toward and whether that matches your surface. This guide explains what each chemical is, how to read a label, and which to buy for each part of the house.
quickAnswer: Pick a silane-rich sealer or blend for dense concrete exposed to salt and freeze-thaw. Pick a siloxane-rich sealer or blend for brick, block, stucco and other porous masonry. When the job mixes surfaces, a silane-siloxane blend covers both, and good blends are commonly rated for 5 to 10 years outdoors.

sections.heading: Silane vs Siloxane: The Short Answer
sections.body:
| Surface | Better choice | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Concrete driveway, sidewalk, steps | Silane or silane-rich blend | Small molecule reaches deeper into tight pores |
| Troweled garage apron | Silane-rich | Very dense surface |
| Brick wall or chimney | Siloxane or siloxane-rich blend | Bridges large pores, strong beading |
| Concrete block above grade | Siloxane-rich blend | Very porous, soaks up rain fast |
| Pavers and mixed surfaces | Blend | Covers both pore sizes |

**Short answer:** silane is the small molecule that goes deep, siloxane is the larger one that stays nearer the surface, and both leave no film. Depth is what protects concrete from salt, so silane takes dense slabs. Pore bridging and beading are what protect open masonry from rain, so siloxane takes brick and block.

Neither changes the look of the surface, neither stops oil well, and neither will hold back water pushing through a basement wall. Those limits matter as much as the differences between them. If you just want a product recommendation for a slab, our [best concrete sealer](/best-concrete-sealer/) picks are mostly blends.

sections.heading: What Is a Siloxane Sealer?
sections.body:
A siloxane sealer is a penetrating water repellent made from short chains of silicon-based molecules, called oligomers, that have already partly reacted before they go in the can. Applied to masonry, they soak into the pores, finish reacting there and bond to the mineral surfaces, leaving the pore walls water-repellent.

### How it behaves

Because the molecules are larger, siloxanes do not travel as far into dense concrete as silanes do. They concentrate closer to the surface, which is where they produce strong, visible beading. They are also less volatile, so less of the product evaporates before it reacts, and they react readily even where conditions are not ideal.

### Where it fits

That combination suits brick, split-face and standard concrete block, stucco and many natural stones. These materials have wide pores that a small molecule can pass through without fully lining. Siloxane spans those openings and stays put.

### What it does not do

A siloxane sealer does not form a coating, does not add gloss and does not fill cracks. The treated surface still breathes, so water vapor can escape while liquid water and dissolved salts are pushed back. That breathability is the main reason repellents outlast film sealers on walls that get moisture from behind.

sections.heading: What Is a Silane Sealer?
sections.body:
A silane sealer is a penetrating repellent built from single, very small silicon-based molecules, usually alkyl alkoxysilanes. Their size lets them travel deep into the fine capillaries of well-finished concrete before reacting.

### How it reacts

Once inside, silane reacts with moisture in the pores, a reaction the high alkalinity of cement helps along, and links into a water-repellent silicone resin anchored to the pore walls. Nothing forms on the surface, and the concrete looks the same as before.

### Why labels list high percentages

Silane molecules are small and somewhat volatile, so some can evaporate before they react, especially on hot or windy days. Products often carry a high share of active material for that reason. Highway-grade silanes are commonly sold at around 40 percent active content or more, which is where queries like "40 percent silane" come from.

### Where it shines

Transportation agencies specify silane-based sealers for bridge decks and highway concrete exposed to deicing salt because depth keeps chlorides away from the top layer, where freeze-thaw damage starts. A home driveway, garage apron or salted sidewalk faces the same chemistry at a smaller scale.

sections.heading: How Do Silane and Siloxane Compare Side by Side?
sections.body:
The table shows general tendencies. Real products vary with concentration, carrier and additives, so use it to read a label, then confirm on the technical data sheet.

| Property | Silane | Siloxane |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Molecule | Small, single | Larger, short chain |
| Depth in dense concrete | Deeper | Shallower |
| Porous masonry | Good, may need more product | Very good |
| Surface beading | Moderate | Strong |
| Volatility while applying | Higher | Lower |
| Typical active content | Often high, up to 40 percent or more | Often lower |
| Classic use | Bridges, driveways, parking decks | Brick, block, stucco walls |
| Visible change | None | None |

### Beading is not protection

A surface that beads water dramatically can still let water in at depth if the treatment is shallow. A deeply treated slab with modest beading can resist freeze-thaw very well. Judge a sealer by depth and coverage rate, not by how impressive the beads look the next morning.

### Both handle sunlight well

Both chemistries sit inside the material rather than on top, so neither yellows or peels in sun the way some films do. Repellency fades slowly as the surface wears, which is why tire paths and the bottom step lose protection first.

### Neither stops oil

Both are designed around water and salt. Motor oil still soaks in, though often less deeply. If oil is the main threat, as on a garage floor, you need a coating; see our [garage floor coating](/best-garage-floor-coating/) comparison.

sections.heading: Which Is Better for Driveways and Dense Concrete?
sections.body:
Silane, or a blend that leans toward silane. Dense concrete has very fine pores, especially where it was troweled smooth, and only a small molecule reaches deep enough to keep salty water out of the zone that scales.

### Why depth matters

Scaling happens when salty water soaks into the top few millimeters, freezes and expands. A deeper repellent layer keeps that zone drier through the winter. Shallow treatments can bead well in October and still let meltwater in by February.

### Old or carbonated concrete

Silane relies on the alkalinity and moisture inside the concrete to react. Very old concrete whose surface has carbonated may react a little less readily. A silane-siloxane blend covers that case, because the siloxane portion reacts readily even where conditions are less than ideal.

### Application conditions

Because silane is volatile, hot slabs and wind can carry part of it away before it reacts. Apply in mild weather, early or late in the day, at the full label coverage rate rather than stretching it. Our [how to seal a concrete driveway](/how-to-seal-a-concrete-driveway/) guide covers timing and technique, and the [concrete driveway sealer rankings](/best-concrete-driveway-sealer-reviews/) list products built for salt.

sections.heading: Which Is Better for Brick, Block and Stucco?
sections.body:
Siloxane, or a blend that leans toward siloxane. These materials have far larger pores than poured concrete and absorb rain quickly, and siloxane's larger molecules line those pores and stay near the face where rain hits.

### Vertical walls

Rain runs down a wall. Strong surface repellency helps it shed rather than soak in, which is why siloxane-rich products are common on brick facades, chimneys, above-grade block foundations and stucco. Our [brick sealer picks](/best-brick-sealer-reviews/) and [cinder block sealer reviews](/best-cinder-block-sealer-reviews/) cover products for those surfaces.

### Efflorescence

Older brick and mortar often hold soluble salts that bloom as white efflorescence when water moves through. Cutting water absorption cuts the bloom. Clean the deposits off first, though, because a repellent applied over them locks the haze in place.

### Fix leaks before sealing

A repellent does not repair a leaking wall. Failed mortar joints, cracks, missing flashing and gutters dumping water down the face all need fixing first. Treating a wall with open joints just redirects water into the joints.

### Is it commonly used in the UK?

Yes. Silane and siloxane masonry repellents, including thick cream versions, are widely sold in the UK and Europe for solid brick walls exposed to driving rain. The chemistry and the rules above are the same on either side of the Atlantic.

sections.heading: Why Are Most Sealers a Silane/Siloxane Blend?
sections.body:
Because most homes have both kinds of surface. One product that handles a driveway, a block foundation and a brick step is more useful than two specialized ones. The silane fraction gives depth in dense concrete, and the siloxane fraction gives beading and pore bridging on masonry.

### Reading the label

Labels rarely state the ratio. They usually give total active content, such as a percentage of silane-siloxane, or simply say "blend." When a data sheet cites bridge decks, highways or DOT-style standards, the formula usually leans silane. When it stresses brick, block and stucco, it often leans siloxane.

### Active content matters more than the ratio

For most homeowners, how much active material is in the can matters more than the exact split. A blend at 20 to 40 percent active content generally puts more protection down per coat than one with a few percent, which is part of why premium repellents cost more. Products that do not state any active content often have little and need reapplying sooner. Concentrates such as Ghostshield Siloxa-Tek 8500 are diluted on site, so compare them at their mixed strength.

### Comparing two very different numbers

A label that says 40 percent silane and one that says 7 percent siloxane are not directly comparable. The first is a high-solids silane aimed at dense concrete; the second is a lower-solids product aimed at porous masonry, where less active material is needed to line large pores. Match the product to the surface first, then compare strength within the same type.

### Water or solvent carrier

Water-based blends are low odor and fine near living spaces. Solvent-based blends can penetrate dense concrete a little more easily and tolerate cooler weather, but they smell strongly and face VOC limits in some states. For most DIY work, a water-based blend such as Foundation Armor SX5000 WB is the practical default.

sections.heading: How Are Silicates, Siliconates, Silicones and Acrylics Different?
sections.body:
Penetrating sealer marketing uses several similar names, and they do different jobs. Mixing them up is the most common way to buy the wrong product.

### Silicates

Sodium, potassium and lithium silicates are densifiers. They react with calcium hydroxide in the concrete to form extra binder, hardening the surface and reducing dust. They make concrete less porous but are not strong water repellents on their own.

### Siliconates

Potassium or sodium methyl siliconates are water repellents that react with carbon dioxide in the air. They are often used on porous masonry as economical treatments and generally do not reach as deep as silane in dense concrete.

### Silicone resins

"Silicone" is used loosely. Some older or cheaper masonry treatments are silicone resins dissolved in solvent that leave a thin surface layer instead of reacting deep in the pores. They can work on porous masonry but tend to be shorter-lived and may darken some surfaces.

### Acrylic cure-and-seal products

Products such as W. R. Meadows VOCOMP-25 are acrylic cure-and-seal compounds, not repellents. They form a film that holds moisture in fresh concrete while it cures and leaves a light protective coat. A silane-siloxane is invisible and breathable; an acrylic cure-and-seal is a surface film that wears and needs renewing. They solve different problems and are often used at different stages of a slab's life.

### Using them together

A densifier first and a repellent second is a common pairing on old, sandy driveways: one hardens the surface, the other keeps water and salt out. On sound concrete that only needs water repellency, the repellent alone is enough.

sections.heading: Which Should You Choose for Each Surface?
sections.body:
Start from the material, then confirm the product label lists it. The best penetrating sealer is the one rated for your surface and applied at the label rate.

| Surface | Best chemistry | Reason |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Broom-finished driveway or walk | Silane-rich or blend | Depth against salt and frost |
| Troweled garage apron | Silane-rich | Dense surface needs small molecules |
| Brick wall or chimney | Siloxane-rich or blend | Large pores, vertical shedding |
| Block foundation above grade | Siloxane-rich or blend | Very porous, absorbs rain quickly |
| Pavers | Blend or paver sealer | Mixed density; joint sand needs other products |
| Old, dusty slab | Silicate, then blend | Harden first, then repel |
| Basement wall below grade | Silicate or cementitious coating | Repellents do not stop water under pressure |

### Below-grade walls

Water pushing in from soil outside is not stopped by a repellent sprayed on the inside face. Interior basement treatments are usually silicate-based or cementitious, and real leaks need drainage or crack repair. See our [basement wall sealer](/best-basement-wall-sealer/) picks for those.

### Pavers and natural stone

Many blends are labeled for pavers and stone, but paver owners often want joint stabilization or color enhancement, which a plain repellent does not give. A dedicated [paver sealer](/best-paver-sealer/) is usually the better fit.

### Grout and tile

Grout sealers vary in chemistry. Some are silane or siloxane based, others use fluoropolymers or acrylics. The safety data sheet usually names the active ingredient if the front label does not. For showers and floors, our [grout sealer guide](/best-grout-sealer/) covers products made for that job.

sections.heading: Are Siloxane Sealers Easy to Apply, and How Long Do They Last?
sections.body:
Yes, they are among the easiest sealers to apply, and good silane-siloxane products are commonly rated for about 5 to 10 years on exterior concrete.

### Application basics

Clean the surface, let it dry for the time on the label (often 24 to 48 hours after rain or washing), then spray with a low-pressure pump sprayer. Many makers call for a flood coat that runs a few inches down a wall, or a wet-on-wet second coat on porous surfaces. Roll or broom out puddles on flat slabs so they do not dry shiny. There is no cutting in, no lap marks and no film to bubble.

### The hard part

You cannot see where you have been once it dries. Work in marked sections, keep track of how much product each section takes, and compare that with the label coverage so you are not stretching it too thin.

### Test before you commit

Treat a small patch, let it cure, then sprinkle water across the edge. The treated area should stay light while untreated concrete darkens. That confirms the product works on your surface before you buy enough for the whole job.

### When to reapply

High-traffic areas wear first. Splash water on the busiest spots each fall. When water darkens the surface and soaks in instead of beading, it is time for another coat. Reapplication is simpler than the first round, because you only need to clean, not strip.

mistakes.title: Buying by name instead of by job
mistakes.body: Silane, siloxane, silicate and siliconate sound alike and do different things. A silicate hardens concrete but repels water only modestly. Read the data sheet for what the product does and which surfaces it lists, rather than choosing by the most impressive word on the front label.

mistakes.title: Judging protection by beading
mistakes.body: Dramatic beading the day after application shows surface repellency, not depth. A shallow treatment can bead beautifully and still let salty water into the zone where freeze-thaw damage starts. On driveways and walks, buy a product built for penetration and apply it at the full coverage rate.

mistakes.title: Spraying silane on a hot, windy day
mistakes.body: Silane is volatile, and a hot slab or a stiff breeze can carry part of it away before it reacts. Apply in mild temperatures, in the morning or late afternoon, on a calm day, so the active material stays in the concrete where it belongs.

mistakes.title: Sealing over dirt or efflorescence
mistakes.body: Repellents need clean, open pores. Dirt, mildew and white efflorescence block penetration, and a repellent applied over efflorescence locks the haze in place. Clean with a suitable masonry cleaner, rinse, and let the surface dry completely before you spray.

mistakes.title: Expecting a repellent to stop leaks
mistakes.body: Silane and siloxane reduce absorption through sound concrete and masonry. They do not stop water under pressure or water coming through cracks, failed mortar or missing flashing. Repair the source first, then use the repellent to protect the surrounding material.

faqs.q: What is the difference between silane and siloxane?
faqs.a: Silane is a small, single molecule that penetrates deep into dense concrete, while siloxane is a larger, partly reacted chain that stays nearer the surface and bridges wide pores. Both are penetrating water repellents that leave no film. Silane suits driveways and slabs; siloxane suits brick, block and stucco. Most retail sealers blend the two.

faqs.q: What is siloxane sealer used for?
faqs.a: Siloxane sealer is used mainly to waterproof porous masonry such as brick, concrete block, stucco and some natural stone. It soaks in, lines the pores and makes rain bead off without changing the look of the surface. It is also blended with silane in many concrete sealers to add surface beading to silane's deeper penetration.

faqs.q: Is silane or siloxane better for a driveway?
faqs.a: Silane, or a silane-rich blend, is usually better for a concrete driveway. Its small molecules reach deeper into tight concrete pores, keeping salty meltwater out of the layer that scales in freeze-thaw winters. Most consumer driveway sealers are blends, which pair silane depth with siloxane beading and work well on broom-finished slabs.

Siloxane, or a siloxane-rich blend, is generally better for brick. Its larger molecules bridge brick's wide pores and give strong beading on vertical walls, so rain sheds instead of soaking in. Make sure mortar joints are sound and the brick is clean and free of efflorescence before you apply any repellent.

faqs.q: Do silane siloxane sealers change the look of concrete?
faqs.a: No, standard silane-siloxane sealers leave no visible change: no sheen, no darkening and no film. Some makers sell enhancing versions that darken the surface slightly. If you want gloss or strong color, you need a film sealer such as an acrylic instead, and you accept recoating it every few years.

faqs.q: Can I put an acrylic sealer over a silane siloxane?
faqs.a: Sometimes, but adhesion can suffer, because the repellent pushes away water-based coatings. Some makers allow a topcoat once the repellent has cured or weathered. Check both labels and test a small area with a tape pull before coating the whole surface. If you want a film, it is often simpler to start with one.

faqs.q: Are silane and siloxane sealers safe to use?
faqs.a: Water-based silane-siloxane sealers are low odor and commonly used around homes. Solvent-based versions are flammable and give off strong vapors, so use them outdoors with good airflow and a respirator rated for organic vapors. Cover plants and glass against overspray, and follow the safety data sheet for the specific product.

bottomLine: Silane and siloxane are two sizes of the same idea. Silane is small and goes deep, which makes it the winner on dense concrete facing salt and freeze-thaw. Siloxane is larger and works near the surface, which makes it the winner on brick, block and stucco. Blends combine both, which is why they fill the shelves and suit most homes. Choose by surface, check the active content on the data sheet, clean and dry the surface, apply at the full label rate in mild weather, and confirm with a water test. Just do not ask either one to stop oil, fill cracks or hold back water under pressure.
